sentence: At a day of about an hour and twenty-four minutes the equator moves at 7.9 km/s, the speed of a low orbit; the push outward cancels gravity.
claim: At a day of about 84.5 minutes (1.41 h) the spin cancels gravity at the equator: the ground moves at 7.9 km/s, and today's 0.465 km/s is 1/17 of that.
note: DERIVATION: arithmetic only; not read from any page. OPEN until a person re-does the sum.
derivation: a = g0 => T = 2 pi sqrt(R^3/GM) = 84.5 min = 1.41 h; v = sqrt(GM/R) = 7.91 km/s; today's 0.465 km/s is 1/17 of it.

sentence: Right now, one day lasts twenty-four hours. Or almost: the Earth turns once in twenty-three hours, fifty-six minutes.
claim: The Earth turns once in 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds; its radius is 6,378 km at the equator and 6,357 km at the poles.
note: OPEN: not read by anyone; the value is a candidate from memory. A person must open the sheet and confirm the rotation period and the radii.
derivation: The Earth turns once in 23 h 56 min 4 s (sidereal rotation period 23.9345 h); equatorial radius 6,378.137 km; polar radius 6,356.752 km.

sentence: Standing on the equator, the ground carries you around at about sixteen hundred and seventy kilometers an hour.
claim: The ground at the equator moves at about 1,674 km/h (465 m/s): one trip around the equator divided by the length of a day. That is about 1/17 of the speed needed to orbit.
note: DERIVATION: arithmetic only; not read from any page. OPEN until a person re-does the sum.
derivation: v = 2 pi R / T = 465 m/s = 1,674 km/h from R = 6,378 km and T = 23.934 h; and 7.9 km/s / 0.465 km/s = 17.

sentence: You weigh about a third of a percent less than you would on a planet that did not spin.
claim: The spin makes you about 0.35% lighter today: the outward push of the spin is 0.034 m/s², against gravity's 9.8 m/s².
note: DERIVATION: arithmetic only; not read from any page. OPEN until a person re-does the sum.
derivation: a = (2 pi / T)^2 R = 0.034 m/s^2 against g0 = GM/R^2 = 9.8 m/s^2: 0.35 % lighter.
